items.question: Why did you think distillation was worth revisiting in a tutorial at Google?
items.object: Teaching modern language-model distillation
items.answer:
I usually am an RL researcher generally, and distillation is something like a side quest I've done at Google. But this time around, I guess there has been a lot of progress. If you think about distillation, I think what comes to mind is the 2015 paper from Jeff Hinton and others, which is the seminal work that people referred to. But then since then it's been like a decade, right? And there must be some progress that has happened since then. Especially now we're talking about LLMs. Back then we were talking about classifiers, like people trained on ImageNet and whatnot.

So I thought it would be a good idea to give a tutorial, at least internally at Google. After the tutorial, what I did was I also published part of the slides which were at least based on publicly available information. I thought it would be worth sharing. Some of the new methods which are coming out are inspired by things which look very different than what you typically think of when you think of distillation. I thought that'll be a nice way to just talk about what people typically think of as distillation and what are the latest skits on the block. Maybe some of them make sense, maybe not, but still worthwhile knowing what is possible.

items.question: How do you understand the meaning of distillation in current model research?
items.object: The contemporary meaning of model distillation
items.answer: There's a purist definition, which is the Hinton definition, but I would say the current usage of the term distillation has kind of expanded a little bit. I think also how you do it, right? Usually, let's say the definition is very broad. It says we want to transfer knowledge from an expensive teacher model to a smaller model, and sometimes the model could be the same size. But then this is very broad; it doesn't say how do you transfer the knowledge. Usually people think, “Oh, we'll collect some data from the teacher and then we'll just fine-tune the student on that data,” but that's one way of doing distillation, and there are other ways too. I thought maybe we should talk about that.

The response states that distillation is not limited to fine-tuning a student on data generated by a teacher model.

items.question: Why do you think distillation remains valuable as language models get larger?
items.object: The practical motivation for language-model distillation
items.answer: I guess the motivation for distillation is kind of easy to crack. You would think bigger LMs are usually better, and that was the trend a few years ago, even now. But in practice what you care about is, let's say, the graph which one of the hosts created, which is the graph of cost versus performance. You want something really good but at a really low cost. Even if something is really good but it costs, I don't know, a thousand times more than something else, maybe we're still not going to use that because it's just too expensive for the use cases people care about. There are other use cases: let's say you want to deploy a model in your smartphone; it's just not possible to fit a really, really large model there. That's another challenge, and I think that's why maybe we still care about distillation per se.

items.question: How do you think about the capability-versus-cost tradeoff that motivates LLM distillation?
items.object: LLM distillation and the tradeoff between capability and cost
items.answer: I think it is really the marginal benefit versus cost argument, right? If the marginal benefit in capability is not worth the additional cost to you, then people don't want to use that bigger model. It is very task dependent. Maybe you really want that capability, but sometimes, especially when you're doing things at bulk, maybe it's okay that you're slightly worse off but it's much cheaper. That's maybe one of the reasons. That's why you want to be at the Pareto frontier. I think the other thing is, the capability which we have right now, maybe next year it'll be much cheaper to have that same thing, and that likely is the result of distillation. It's not just because we figured out something magical; distillation can help you bring the cost of any existing capability down.

items.question: How do you interpret the capability–cost Pareto frontier in terms of progress in distillation?
items.object: The capability–cost Pareto frontier as a measure of progress in distillation
items.answer: Yeah, it's a little bit of search too: you go up in capability, then you go down in efficiency to make it more efficient, and that kind of thing. The other thing I noticed as well, which I kind of pointed out, was that the slope of the Pareto frontier is basically the state of the art of distillation, and the gentler the slope, the better distillation is. I thought that's kind of cool.

items.question: Why do you see training a larger teacher model as a worthwhile approach to producing a good small model?
items.object: Training larger teacher models to produce good small models through distillation
items.answer: To train a good small model, maybe it's still better to train a bigger model. That's what you were mentioning earlier also, that maybe that's why we are training teacher models. This kind of finding has still stayed relevant. I would say this is still true, and this is another good motivation for actually thinking about distillation.

items.question: How do you think about designing a model-distillation pipeline around what you want the student model to achieve?
items.object: Designing a model-distillation pipeline
items.answer:
Depends, right? For example, your distilled model could itself be RL. Maybe you want to skip the RL stage. Let's say you have the final model you want to serve, and then you just distill it; maybe you don't need to do anything else after distillation. Think of it as, what do you want out of this? Let's say you say, “Oh no, I just want distillation so that I distill some base capabilities in my model, and then I will still do some sort of specific post-training afterwards.” Then it makes sense to have a different teacher.

I think it depends on what you want out of distillation, because distillation is just saying I can transfer capabilities from this teacher model to the student one. But that's not perfect, right? There's always some gap, so maybe you still want to self-improve that student, and that's what RL is for. I would think maybe an optimal pipeline would look like you do distillation heavily, but then you still do some RL afterwards, because maybe there's still something you can get out of your reward functions or whatever your post-training stack is, at least in my thinking, unless your distillation gets you really, really close to the teacher. At that point you'll be like, “Okay, there's no point doing anything more; let's just do distillation and move on.” That could happen, right, if distillation was that good. Let's say you take the best model out there and you can just distill it, and for the thing you care about, let's say coding, you distill it so well that on coding benchmarks and all the coding tasks you're doing it's really nearly matching the teacher, then why would you do anything else afterwards? It depends on how good distillation is, and that's more of an empirical thing, I would say.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between logit-based distillation and next-token prediction for LLMs?
items.object: Logit-based distillation as generalized next-token prediction
items.answer: For LLMs, I'm doing next-token prediction, except I'm using soft tokens. The objective is the same, except rather than having a single hard token that you're saying, “I want to predict this token next,” I have soft labels: basically some probabilities for each of these tokens, and I'm predicting all of them together. It's a generalized version of next-token prediction, but at the end of the day the loss is exactly the same. The only thing that changes is whether we have one-hot labels, where only one token gets a value of one and everything else zero, or soft labels. This can now be easily used for pre-training. One notable example of this is Gopher? They used distillation for pre-training, where they use logits, or these soft labels, rather than having hard 0-1 tokens. They have soft labels for all possible tokens, and then they just run the next-token prediction loss on this.

items.question: How do you understand why distilling a larger language model can produce a better student than training the student from scratch on the same data?
items.object: Why language-model distillation can outperform training a student from scratch
items.answer:
When I observe some next token in the data, I assume that's ground truth. Here I'm saying, “I'm actually relying on my teacher to tell me what is the possible next token after the sentence,” and then I assume that as ground truth. The objective is the same; the only thing is what information you assume access to, and here we have more information, because I guess the teacher was trained on that human data, but hoping that it generalized. That's the dark knowledge bit: maybe it actually knows more, that maybe there are multiple tokens which are possible, it's just that I only observed one of them in the data. The teacher is telling me there are these few tokens that are very likely after the sentence, so maybe I should be trying to predict all of these. That is when maybe the magic of distillation is from.

You can see in these plots, this is the kind of dark knowledge we're talking about. If you train the student model from scratch, that's always worse. Higher is perplexity, so higher perplexity is worse. There's no change; I have the same data and everything. The only thing is whether I'm training this model from scratch or distilling using a bigger model on that data, and you see the effect of distillation actually doing better. That's the reason maybe people do distillation. It's not just cost savings; maybe you're getting a better student model at the end of the day. You couldn't have just done it if you were to do scratch training for that.

Here you're saying, “I'm actually relying on my teacher to tell me what is the possible next token after the sentence or this part of this,” and then you assume that as ground truth. The objective is the same; the only thing is what information you assume access to, and here we have more information, because I guess the teacher was trained on that human data, but hoping that it generalized. items.question: How do you think training compute should be accounted for when comparing a distilled model with a model trained from scratch?
items.object: Compute-matched evaluation of distillation
items.answer: I think there's definitely more compute. I don't know if the Gemma 2 folks reported in the report, was it compute matched or was it data matched? That's a very good comparison: you should ideally be comparing on compute, whether if you do more updates on the same data, which matches, let's say, the amount of compute used.

items.question: Why do you see synthetic-data distillation as such a useful method for LLMs?
items.object: Synthetic-data distillation for LLMs
items.answer:
The nice thing about this method is it only needs API access. You can take any model out there and just prompt that model, generate outputs, and then use that data. You have some prompts, you take your teacher model, generate some outputs, and then you do supervised fine-tuning on this data. That's the simplest thing possible you can do, and it's also a very common method.

This is exactly the same loss that we were optimizing earlier with the principal distillation, like the KL divergence. It's just a different way of doing it, so it is a very principled objective. It is minimizing some sort of divergence or KL divergence between my teacher distribution q and the student, and it's just a different way of doing it where I am basically sampling something from the teacher and fine-tuning the student on this. Here we don't assume access to any sort of logits or next-token probability distributions. We are just sampling from a teacher, and that's the only access we assume, and then we fine-tune the student on that data. Same loss, different way of optimizing it, and it just turns out to be simpler, so that's why everyone uses it.

One nice thing about this kind of distillation is it doesn't matter if you have vocabulary mismatch, because we're not using the next-token distribution or probability labels. You can distill from one model which uses some random tokenizer to another model. That's a very good feature. That's why they were able to distill from DeepSeek model to Llama or Qwen, and you don't have to even think about that tokenizer. You just need an API, collect data, fine-tune the student model on that data, and you're done. You can already get pretty close.

Logits are definitely assuming access to more information, so it can be. But then again you don't have access to logits if you want to distill a black-box model. No one wants—it's not legal, I guess, to distill some model, or at least the terms and conditions don't allow you to do that. But for open models, yeah, you can do better because you have access to logits, so why not use them? At least that's my take.

items.question: How would you improve sample selection when using synthetic data to distill a model?
items.object: Best-of-N and retaining top-K samples in synthetic-data distillation
items.answer:
A better version of this is you can do something like best-of-N, which was used in DeepSeek. If you saw that paper, they trained the DeepSeek Reasoner model and then distilled that model to other models. What they did was they took the best model they had, generated a bunch of samples, filtered them based on correctness, because these were tasks like coding, mathematical problem solving, and a bunch of those things. They saw which outputs actually get the right answer or pass the test cases, picked those, and fine-tuned the model on that data.

When you're doing best-of-N, why not keep the top K rather than just the top one? If you're already generating a lot of samples, why throw away—if you have some sort of scoring mechanism of how good something is. This thing is called MBR in the translation literature. The key idea is very simple: just don't throw away everything; use the top K samples rather than just the top one. This might be better, and that's true. That's a simple thing worth trying if people are doing synthetic data distillation. There's small gains: if MBR is using just the top one, and then if you increase to top 10, top 20, top 40, you can see slight gains as you use more samples.

items.question: How do you think about choosing between a smaller and a larger teacher model when your synthetic-data generation budget is fixed?
items.object: Choosing smaller versus larger teachers under a fixed synthetic-data generation budget
items.answer:
The simple idea is that if you have two models, there's a sampling cost you're paying. You can generate data from a really big model, or generate data from a smaller model, but a lot more of it, because both of those use the same compute. The sampling cost in FLOPs is proportional to the number of parameters in the model times the number of inference tokens. There are some assumptions here; I'm assuming we're using KV cache, but assume this mental model that the cost is proportional to number of parameters times number of tokens. For a fixed number of tokens, if you have a much smaller model, let's say Llama 70B versus Llama 7B, you can generate ten times more data in principle.

If we have access to some sort of filtering function or reward function, then it becomes even more interesting, because now you can filter this data too. One thing we found consistently: here we had two models, Gemma 9B and Gemma 27B, and we found consistently that generating data from 9B in a compute-matched setting is always better, even better for distilling or actually improving the 27B model itself. We're fine-tuning the bigger 27B model. There are two things we can do: generate data from the 27B model and filter that and fine-tune it, so that's self-improvement using some sort of reward function; or generate data from the smaller 9B model, just generate a lot more of it and fine-tune the 27B. We found that's better to do.

The magic is because we can generate a lot more samples, and we have a way to actually select what is a good sample, because we're doing this on reasoning, like math and coding, so we can filter that. If you do cost matched—I was so far talking about compute matched, but if you think about API pricing, let's say we have two models, Gemini Pro and Gemini Flash. The pricing of Flash is 35 times cheaper than Pro, and now actually it's even better to generate data from Flash for the tradeoff you get, because you can generate 30 to 35 times more data for the same cost. If you have some dollar budget of $100, you can generate samples from these two models, and it turns out that actually just generating a lot more data from Flash and filtering that would be much better. These are all results on some math reasoning benchmarks; I think it's Hendrycks math.

items.question: How do you understand the exposure-bias problem in supervised distillation?
items.object: Exposure bias in supervised distillation and behavior cloning
items.answer:
If you think about distillation, or generally just next-token prediction, there is a mismatch at training time and test time or inference time. At training time we are basically training on a fixed data set of outputs. I already give you the output and you fine-tune on that. That's what was being done in synthetic data distillation: I already gave you some input and output, and you just supervised fine-tune on that data. But at test time the student model itself is generating tokens one by one autoregressively. This is also the same difference which happens in SFT versus RL. In SFT you're teaching it to copy something; in RL it's learning what to do using a reward function. There's a big difference and there is a mismatch at fine-tuning time and inference time. It's called exposure bias. This is another term for this mismatch in the NLP community, but all that there is to it is this train-inference mismatch.

This inference mismatch is very common in the RL community. This work was done back when people were trying to copy agents, which might be relevant now again. You can do behavior cloning or supervised fine-tuning, which is very common, but other folks figured out a much better way; they call it DAgger. Imagine what's going on: you're training a student model on some fixed data distribution. At test time the student model makes a mistake. Here, let's say the student is learning how to drive a car, and all the student was trained on is how the teacher is driving the car. There are scenarios the teacher would never do because the teacher is a good driver, so maybe he'll never run into really bad situations. But the student might run into such situations. Let's say I see some tree and I'm going to crash into that. The teacher is never going to show you such a scenario, because generally the teacher is a good driver, and if you collect data from that teacher they'll just show you what good driving looks like. That means you cannot recover from these things: if the student is going to crash into something, it has not seen this kind of data before. It hasn't seen, “Oh, if I made this kind of mistake, what do I do?” The learner is falling off the cliff and the teacher just never goes there. This is a common problem that also happens in RL or any sort of agentic task.

items.question: What do you find compelling about applying on-policy distillation to language models?
items.object: RL-inspired on-policy distillation for language models
items.answer:
This is the default approach people use when they are distilling in self-driving-style situations or other agentic situations. This is a method from 2010 or something, designed for RL agents. We thought, well, we can close our eyes and think of LLMs as agents, and eventually LLMs will become agents, but LLMs are also producing token by token, and maybe we can think of these as actions. They are doing things and then we want feedback on, “Oh, is this good enough or not?” You can assume the similar methodology can be applied.

The fix is very simple. The main change is rather than sampling the output sequences from the teacher, we sample that from the student itself. The student is sampling these tokens or sequence of words for text, or whatever. Now we run inference using the teacher on these tokens, and this can be parallelized. Once you sample the sequence from the student, you can just send the entire sequence to the teacher and then you can get logits for all of this. This is just running inference, so this is not autoregressive; you just send it in parallel and get logits, and then you minimize the logits. The only main difference is you're sampling data from the student rather than the teacher. What it looks like is basically at every point in time I'm asking the teacher, “Hey, what do you think about this? Do you think this is good enough? Would you have done this or would you have done something else?” At every point in time the student is asking the teacher for feedback, and the teacher is going, “I will not do this; I'll do this instead,” and the student says, “Okay, I guess I'll keep that in mind.” It's getting this kind of correction feedback. Imagine if you're really close to colliding into a tree, the teacher would say, “Actually do this thing so that you avoid this collision,” or before it's actually even going to the collision, the teacher would say, “I'll never do this kind of thing; do something else.”

The nice thing is this basically means there's no train-test mismatch. The way we're generating the data is also the same thing done at test time: at training time the student is generating the data autoregressively, and at test time the student is again generating the data autoregressively. There is no train-test mismatch of that sort. That's the main fix, this kind of on-policy approach. One interesting detail afterwards: you can derive this. All you need to do, at least in math, is flip the direction of your KL. Earlier we minimized KL between a teacher and student model. If we just swap that order, because KL is not symmetric, you will get this kind of distillation. That's nice, cute math you can write to say, “Oh, actually I can derive this,” and this is very principled, it's not a hack.

The other nice thing is you don't have to do full RL. You can sample from the student and optimize some loss. You don't have to backprop through the sampling distribution, because that also depends on student parameters; that becomes full RL. There's another paper on that, but if you still want to do supervised training and you're only changing which data distribution you care about, we're saying we care about the data distribution with student samples, because that's what we want to use at test time. That's the other trick people have done in the RL literature. We are saying what if we just do that again with language models? This was a paper we wrote in 2024, saying there's a neat way of doing distillation which other people use all the time; what if you try that for language models? That works very well.

items.question: How do you decide whether teacher logits are worth using for language-model distillation?
items.object: Using teacher logits for language-model distillation
items.answer: I would generally say if you have more information, usually it's probably better to use it. It might be a capacity thing. Look at the T5 base model: how many parameters, 250 million? That's not even a language model at this point, we consider; that's micro size, because people call 0.5 billion tiny, and this was a base model back in the day. I would say it depends heavily on the capacity to some extent. My opinion still is, if you can use logits and it's not too inconvenient, probably worth it. Maybe your method is not as good, and again the method which we are competing against is a method developed in 2015, the synthetic, the logits distillation thing, the supervised KD. Better methods like the green one can easily make logits much more useful. I would say that's maybe the blocker with logits, and more research would be really helpful there. Anyway, my answer is use logits if you have them.

items.question: How do you think about choosing the direction of KL divergence when distilling a larger teacher into a smaller student?
items.object: KL-divergence direction and the diversity–performance tradeoff in distillation
items.answer:
I think this is worth internalizing. When you're doing distillation there's always a model capacity mismatch: the student model is generally much smaller than the teacher model. Now it depends on which direction of KL you optimize; it changes what the student would learn. Here it's a very idealized scenario where I have a bimodal Gaussian distribution, and then the student model is a unimodal Gaussian, which means I can only fit one of the peaks. Depending on which direction of KL I optimize, I have very different behavior. These are called mode-covering and mode-seeking KL. Typically what we use is this mode-covering KL, the standard distillation loss everyone uses. What's weird about it: it's putting a lot of mass on places where there's no mass put by the teacher. The teacher would not sample anything in that regime where the peak of the green curve is, but that is exactly the behavior you're getting when you optimize this direction of KL. With the other one, it's covering one of the peaks but putting no mass at all on other parts of the distribution. This is called mode-seeking. That's the difference in these two directions. Supervised KD minimizes the direction of KL between teacher and student, while on-policy distillation minimizes the other direction. It's basically saying I'm happy fitting one of the modes, or getting one way of getting this capability right, rather than getting all these different ways of getting the capability right. If capacity is a constraint, you can see why there is a difference in divergence used.

This is a very exaggerated example. Obviously most actual text doesn't look like that. Also, this is Gaussians; this is like saying if the world was perfect and pictures looked like Gaussians. In practice you get a tradeoff between diversity and performance. Depending on the KL divergence you use, you get a tradeoff. If you use one direction of KL, you get pretty high diversity or low similarity but low performance. On the other end you have high performance but low diversity or high similarity. For any task you care about, I would say you'll have the same kind of tradeoff. The general recommendation I would give people is maybe use a mixture, half and half. That's what some people have used, basically saying, “I don't know what I want, I just want something to work well enough. I'll do half and half and hope that it works out.” Generally it would, I think. There are different ways of mixing half and half; this is one way, Jensen-Shannon divergence is another. This is just our way to say, “I don't know what I want; let me just do this and hope it works,” and usually it does.

items.question: How do you approach implementing distillation using an existing RL framework?
items.object: Implementing distillation with an RL framework
items.answer: There are basically three easy steps to do this thing. First step is I go to an RL framework, whatever framework I have; I turn off the reward term, so I delete the reward part of it. All I'm left with is some KL term. Then I swap the KL, the anchor policy, to a bigger teacher policy, and there you go, I've implemented the distillation we're talking about. RL is already doing two things: it's doing reward maximization subject to some KL constraint. The KL constraint is usually to the same policy as the student or some SFT policy, but it doesn't have to be; it could be a bigger model.

items.question: How do you understand the connection between speculative decoding and distillation?
items.object: The connection between speculative decoding and distillation
items.answer: The small model is doing speculative decoding. The bigger model checks whether the tokens it generates match the small model's tokens. That's very similar to what we are doing. If you think of the bigger model as a teacher, then the smaller model is just sampling some tokens and then asking the teacher, “Do you think this is good?” There is this connection between speculative decoding and this kind of distillation. The main difference is in speculative decoding you just accept or reject the whole sequence. Here you can use logits and do something more fine-grained, so it becomes a training signal. That's one fun connection.

items.question: What do you think matters most when choosing a distillation process?
items.object: Tradeoffs in choosing a distillation process
items.answer: I think this is maybe one of the most important things to consider when people are thinking about distillation, because they have to make some of these decisions: what do they have? Do they care about training quite quickly, or do they want a process where they just have to do this once and that's it, they never have to come back to it again? Based on that, tradeoffs are very different. More recently, when thinking about agentic tasks or long-horizon tasks, that's where maybe things are even more interesting, because maybe it looks very different from what distillation has been done for, let's say, small, few-thousand-token tasks versus hundreds-of-thousands-of-tokens tasks. Those I think might have very different behavior.

items.question: How do you decide whether more complex distillation methods are worth the additional compute and complexity?
items.object: The value of more complex, compute-intensive distillation methods
items.answer:
I think it depends on how valuable the task is. I guess it's a question of: would a 10% jump in capability matter? This is something someone told me and I kind of internalized. They said, “You distill a model once, but you serve it billions of times.” I realized what they're trying to say is it's worth spending the additional compute now, because if this model is the model which you're going to serve to lots and lots of people, maybe it's worth the extra capability improvement.

But then again, it really depends on how much capability is the threshold. I would say try the simplest thing first, which is synthetic data distillation. That already gets you to 80% or 90% of the job, and now the question to ask is, is this good enough or do we want to do more? That's where you decide whether you want to do these more complex distillation things, which have this inference. My answer is oftentimes we do, because if we can push that Pareto frontier really up and be like, “Oh, we can serve you really, really good capabilities but at a really cheap cost,” that's how these newer, better distillation methods can come into the picture. Hopefully it's only done once; you're not doing it again and again. The point is it depends on how valuable this model is, and whether making this model twice as better but with the same cost is meaningful enough and worth the additional complexity. I would say always try the simple thing first and then decide whether it's worthwhile doing the more complicated thing. Sometimes it is, sometimes it's not.

items.question: Why do you think logits distillation could help small reasoning models close the gap with their largest teachers?
items.object: Logits distillation for reasoning models
items.answer: I would say synthetic data distillation would get pretty far, and people are mostly working on that. My hunch is that logits distillation can go even further, and you might be able to even close the gap with the biggest of the teachers you have, because I don't think you need a huge number of parameters. Reasoning process is very long sequence, right? At the end of the day the model is producing these thoughts, and to reason really well maybe it's not about capacity, it's about using this inference-time compute well. My hunch is synthetic distillation would go very far, but a better distillation method can maybe even start getting to close the gap, and you might have a very strong small reasoner. That will be a big uplift.

items.question: How would you decide whether a reasoning model warrants a more complex distillation method?
items.object: Choosing a distillation method for a reasoning model
items.answer: People are not trying it because we don't have access to logits; it's annoying to use. If you try to distill from DeepSeek, you can't serve that huge model and have a live teacher running, because it is going to be expensive. But then again, maybe some people can afford to do that and it's worth trying to push that and see if we can push much further. The results I showed you earlier basically on math tasks, we're able to close the gap reasonably well. On coding there was a huge gap still after synthetic data distillation. How do you bridge that gap? There are easy ways: either you collect a lot more data, a lot more prompts, that's obviously a simple way to go about it; or you try to use your existing data and annotate this with logits; that's supervised distillation. Or you go the extra mile and say, “Let me just generate data from my student and ask my teacher model to see what happens.” I don't know the answer, but I feel like that is where it depends on how good of a student you want; that will dictate what kind of distillation method you use. Likely for most people maybe the simple method suffices, but I'm guessing if you want your model to be much better than others, and that is maybe the winning edge you have, then it's worthwhile pushing for that extra, because there's a one-time complexity cost. We already are paying that when we're doing RL, so it's not that big of a cost, honestly.

items.question: How do you think people should approach established methods when trying to improve their work in AI?
items.object: Questioning established methods
items.answer: My call to action is mostly: assume things are suboptimal and we can do better. Think about what method we are using and how old that is, and very likely you'll find, “Oh, we have been using this kind of okay thing. It's simple, that's why everyone's using it, but it's not really good.” Usually that helps you. Even if you are doing something really good, you might end up finding something better. I think that's a good hunch for people, even when you're doing practical things. Don't get satisfied easily; ask these questions: why am I happy with this, and can I do better? Usually if you start asking these questions, I think you move further along.

items.question: What value do you see in using research discovery tools to connect current AI work with older research?
items.object: Research discovery tools and connections to older reinforcement learning research
items.answer: One problem I have in AI is there's too many things going on, a lot of cool stuff. It's very hard to find the cool stuff, and a lot gets lost in this. Finding some of these cool things is going to be very important in the coming years, to connect the dots and maybe try out the relevant things. I saw the deep research-style podcast, but use those kinds of tools a lot, and maybe that will help you make the connections you need. You still have to do a lot of your own thinking, but finding some of these things—for example, the kind of things I presented were mostly saying people used to do this thing in RL this way; we are doing LMs now, but we're not using any of the things RL people used to do. What if we just do that? Suddenly you have a much better method. That kind of thing helps, especially when we are talking about things like agents and reasoning. A lot of the things are probably done on a small scale in the literature, in games and whatnot, and a lot of those ideas would be relevant again now. It's just worth thinking about which ones.
